worked.scenario: A true-breeding dark plant is crossed with a true-breeding pale plant. All F1 plants are dark; some F2 offspring are pale.

An F2 dd offspring expresses pale, explaining reappearance without blending or a new mutation.

worked.title: Solve a two-locus cross without unnecessary boxes
worked.scenario: In an independent complete-dominance model, RrTt × rrTt produces offspring. Find the probability of red, short offspring: R_tt.
steps: At the colour locus, Rr × rr gives P(R_) = 1/2.
At the height locus, Tt × Tt gives P(tt) = 1/4.
Both conditions are required, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.
For 80 offspring the expected count is 80 × 1/8 = 10.
The result relies on independence of the two loci.

protectedBlocks.exactHtml:
Optional video support

Two-trait crosses and independent assortment — video support

As you watch: List valid gametes for two loci, use a Punnett square or product rule, and identify the assumption of independent assortment.

Optional video. Internet access is required. The explanation below covers the idea without the video.

Open on YouTube

Read the explanation

For AaBb × AaBb, the A locus gives a 3/4 dominant-phenotype probability and 1/4 recessive probability. The B locus gives the same. If the loci assort independently, the probability of both dominant phenotypes is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. The other phenotype combinations are 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16, producing the familiar 9:3:3:1 expectation. This ratio is specific to the stated heterozygote cross and allele relationships. For a different cross, recompute. In AaBb × aaBb, probability of A_ is 1/2 and probability of B_ is 3/4, so both dominant phenotypes have probability 3/8. A memorized 9/16 would be wrong.
